entries.question: Does the site visit cost anything?
entries.answer:
No. The first site visit is free. Someone comes out, walks the property with you, looks at access, grade, drainage and what is already growing there, and talks through what you want. Booking it commits you to nothing.

Two things are worth knowing before it happens. The visit is a working conversation rather than a sales call, and it is also where GMZ works out whether this is a project we are the right contractor for, so expect direct questions about scope, timing and what you are planning to spend. And a visit is not a bid. What can come out of it is a shared understanding of the work and, when it makes sense, a complimentary concept and a planning range to think about.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm the site consultation stays free and that this can be stated publicly. It is free today but nothing is written down. Also decide whether a charge applies to properties outside the regular service area, or to a second trip on the same lead. Note that the free-visit statement also appears in 'Is the concept free' and 'Ballpark over the phone'; if it changes, all three change together.

entries.question: How soon can someone come out and look at my yard?
entries.answer:
It depends on the week, and you will get an actual date rather than a promise that someone will call you back. Tell us your town and what you want done, and you will hear what is genuinely open. Landscape work here runs on the weather, so spring books up faster than late fall.

If your project has a date attached to it, say so on that first call: an event, a house going on the market, a permit clock, a school year, a family visit. It changes what can honestly be promised, and it is far better known at the start than discovered halfway through.
entries.decisionNote: Decide whether to publish a typical scheduling window for site visits, for example "usually within two weeks." No such commitment exists today, so this answer promises a real date on the call instead of a lead time. If a window is published it has to be one the schedule can actually hold.

entries.question: Which towns do you work in?
entries.answer:
GMZ works the San Francisco Peninsula and is based in Redwood City. The towns we work in regularly are Redwood City, Atherton, Menlo Park, Palo Alto, Woodside, San Carlos, Belmont, Portola Valley, Los Altos and Hillsborough.

If you are near that list but not on it, ask. For a build project a little extra distance is usually workable, because the crew parks once in the morning and works the same ground all day. For maintenance it matters more: maintenance runs on fixed-day routes, so a property well away from an existing route may not be one we can serve properly. We would rather tell you that than take the account and become the contractor who keeps arriving late.

entries.question: What size projects do you take? Is my job too small?
entries.answer:
There is no published minimum job size, so ask about your job rather than talk yourself out of calling. GMZ does full residential design and build work: planting, irrigation, drainage, patios, walls, fences and lighting. It also runs a maintenance book of weekly and biweekly accounts, so work that is too small to mobilize a build crew for is often better handled as a maintenance visit or a short service call.

What decides it is not square footage. It is whether the work justifies bringing a crew, a truck and equipment to your property at all. An afternoon of pruning and a new patio are different kinds of job, not different sizes of the same job, and they are priced and contracted differently.

Say what you want done on the first call and you will get a straight answer, including "that is not the right fit for us" if that is the answer. A contractor who takes a job that is wrong for them serves it badly, and you feel it in the schedule.
entries.decisionNote: Set the "projects typically start at" figure for design/build and confirm whether it gets published. No number exists today and this answer deliberately names none. Also confirm the routing rule for small work: sent to maintenance, taken as a one-off service call, or declined.

entries.question: Are you licensed and insured?
entries.answer:
Yes. GMZ Landscaping Inc. is a licensed California landscape contractor, and our CSLB license number is published on this site so you can check it yourself. Look it up on the Contractors State License Board website, which shows the license status, the classification, and the bond and workers' compensation records on file. It is free, it takes about a minute, and it is worth doing for every contractor you are considering, not only this one.

If you need a certificate of insurance for an HOA, a property manager or your own file, ask and one will be sent to you. We work out of a P.O. Box rather than a storefront, which is normal for a landscape contractor; the license number is the thing to verify us by.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm what insurance language may be published. The only confirmed credential is the CSLB license, so the draft's flat claim that GMZ "carries general liability and workers' compensation coverage" has been removed and replaced with the public license record plus a certificate on request. Confirm current general liability and workers' compensation status, the carrier, and whether a certificate can be promised on request, before any coverage sentence goes back on the site. The license number itself stays in site data and is not retyped into this answer.

entries.question: What actually happens when I call?
entries.answer:
A short conversation, then a decision about whether a site visit makes sense for both of us. Expect to be asked what you want done, where the property is, when you would like it done, who else is part of the decision, and what you are planning to spend. That last question is the one people brace for, and it is asked as much for your benefit as ours: it is how you find out early whether GMZ is in the right range for your project, rather than after a design is already underway.

You will not get a price on that call. Landscape work is priced off a measured site and chosen materials, and anyone pricing your yard over the phone is guessing at both. What you can get on the call is whether this is work GMZ does, whether your property is in the area we serve, and a date to walk it.

entries.question: Do I need to have drawings or a plan before I call you?
entries.answer:
No. Most people call with photos and a rough idea, and that is enough to start. If you already have drawings from an architect or a landscape designer, GMZ can build to them; bring them to the visit and you will get an honest read on whether they are buildable as drawn and what is missing. If you have nothing, GMZ designs as well as builds, and the design step is its own paid stage under its own signed agreement.

What is needed before a firm price is a measured site and decided materials, and that is exactly what the design step produces. It is also why a number given before that point is a planning range rather than a bid. Nobody can price a yard accurately from photographs, and a contractor who says otherwise is guessing with your money.

entries.question: What should I send you before you come out?
entries.answer:
Photos and a few plain facts, sent ahead, make the visit much more useful. Send photos of the whole area from several angles, including the parts you are unhappy with, and anything you have already collected: a plot plan or survey, drawings from an architect or designer, HOA rules that apply to your yard, and pictures of yards you like.

Two details are worth writing down because they change the work more than people expect. First, how a truck and a small machine would reach the work area, and how wide the narrowest gate is. Second, whether water collects anywhere after rain. Also useful: what you want kept, and what you have already decided versus what is still open.

For a maintenance account it is simpler. Photos of the property, whether there is an irrigation system and roughly how it is set up, and which day of the week suits you. None of this is required. If you would rather just talk, call and bring the rest to the visit.

entries.question: Why won't you just give me a price?
entries.short: Why a range, not a price
entries.answer:
Because nobody has measured your property yet, and a single number before that would be a guess dressed up as a commitment. The first number you get from GMZ is a range. It is built from a walk of the site, photos and rough dimensions, not from a measured survey and a final materials list. Those two things move a landscape price more than anything else, and neither is settled at this point.

Here is how much they move it. The surface material you choose can move the biggest part of the price a long way, and the same patio in a different material is a different project financially. What sits under the existing surface, and whether a truck can reach the back of the property, changes the labor before a single thing is installed. We can tell you the honest window your project sits in today. We cannot hand you a fixed price for work that has not been drawn or measured, and a number given before that work is done usually turns into a change order later.

The number tightens as the site is measured and the materials are chosen. Measuring costs you nothing.

entries.question: Can you just give me a ballpark over the phone?
entries.answer:
Not a number, no. A price given by someone who has not seen your property is either useless or misleading, and it tends to become the figure you remember for the rest of the project. We would rather not start you there.

What a phone call is good for is deciding quickly whether we are a fit. If what you are describing and what you want to spend are not in the same neighborhood, we will say so on the call rather than after the drive. If they are, we book a visit. The visit is free, and it is where the useful conversation actually happens.

If you are asking about maintenance rather than a build, the answer is the same for the same reason: we walk the property first. Maintenance is priced separately from construction work and runs under its own service agreement, with its own schedule and its own terms.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm two things: (1) whether GMZ publishes a "projects start at" figure so callers can self qualify before the call, and what that figure is, since none exists today and none may be invented; (2) whether the site consultation stays free, which this answer states outright.

entries.question: How wide is the range going to be, and why so wide?
entries.answer:
It is wide, and we would rather be plain about that than pretend otherwise. At the concept stage the top of the range sits well above the bottom, because the two things that decide the final number have not happened yet: nobody has measured the site, and you have not chosen the materials. Both of those are real work, and doing them properly is what closes the gap.

The range narrows in steps. It narrows when we measure. It narrows when you pick a surface material and a plant palette. It narrows when we know whether the existing surface comes out and where the debris goes, and again when current prices come back on the specific items in your plan. Once there is a measured plan and selected materials, the number is tight enough to commit to, and that is the point at which we put a fixed price in front of you.

We will also tell you which parts of your range are the loose ones. Usually it is demolition, drainage and anything underground, because what is beneath the surface is unknown until somebody digs.

entries.question: Is the planning budget a quote?
entries.answer:
No. It is a planning number, not a bid and not a fixed price, and the document says exactly that on its face. GMZ calls it a Preliminary Budget and Scope Acknowledgment. Its job is to tell you what to plan around, and to put the scope in writing so we are both looking at the same project.

What it is: a range for the work described, broken into the areas of your property so you can see where the money sits. What it is not: an offer we are bound to, a price we can hold, or a promise about work nobody has measured. A number you can sign comes later, after a measured plan and chosen materials.

We work this way because a planning budget is the only honest thing to hand someone who needs to know what to expect before they have bought a design. The alternative is a firm-sounding number written over an unmeasured yard, and the person holding the difference in that arrangement is you.

entries.question: If I accept the planning budget, what have I committed to?
entries.answer:
Nothing. Acknowledging the planning budget is not a contract to build and it does not obligate you to spend anything. You are confirming three things: that you have seen the scope we described, that you understand the number is a planning range rather than a fixed price, and that you would like to keep going.

It exists to prevent one specific problem, which is two people remembering the scope differently three months later. Everything we priced is listed. Everything we did not price is listed as well, and that second list is the one worth reading slowly, because it is where most disputes in this trade actually live.

The next commitment is a separate document and it is a real one: the design agreement, which is signed and paid. The construction contract is separate again, and comes after that. Nothing before those two obligates you to build anything.

entries.question: Is the concept really free, or is there a catch?
entries.answer:
It is complimentary today, and there is no catch attached to it. Before you buy any design work, GMZ will walk your property, put together a concept for what could happen there, and give you a planning budget to go with it. You are not billed for that and you are not obliged to go further.

What is not free is the design itself. The measured plans, the material selections and the drawings a crew can actually build from are paid work, under their own signed design agreement. That step is priced as a percentage of construction, in a band of 10 to 15 percent. The design fee is not credited back against the construction price, and we say so plainly because most people assume the opposite. It pays for design time, which is real time by real people, and it has value whether or not GMZ ends up building the project.

The concept exists so you can decide whether this project is worth designing at all. If the answer is no, you have spent nothing.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm two things before this publishes: (1) whether the concept and planning budget stay complimentary or become a small paid first phase of the design agreement, and if paid, the fee, since no figure exists and none may be invented; (2) whether the site consultation stays free, which this answer also states. This is the canonical decision on the free concept and free visit: the same statements appear in 'Does the site visit cost anything', 'Ballpark over the phone', 'Why do I have to pay for a design' and 'Maintenance client, new project', and all of them move together.

entries.question: What if the budget comes back higher than I was expecting?
entries.answer:
Say so, and tell us the number you had in mind. That is a normal conversation and it is far better to have it now than after a design has been drawn to a scope you cannot fund. A planning budget that lands above your expectation is doing its job: it found the gap while closing it is still cheap.

There are three usual ways to close it. The first is scope: take something out or make it smaller. A smaller paved area, fewer built structures, planting instead of a hard surface. The second is material choice, which is the biggest single lever on most projects, because the same design in a different surface material is a different price. The third is phasing the work over time, which we cover separately.

What we will not do is quietly thin the work to hit a number. Cutting base depth, drainage or soil preparation makes a job cheaper on paper and more expensive in a few years, and you are the one who pays that second bill. If a scope genuinely cannot be built properly for your budget, we would rather tell you than take the job.

entries.question: Can we do the project in phases to spread the cost?
entries.answer:
Yes, and it is common. Phasing is a real option rather than a consolation prize. It works best when every phase is drawn on one plan at the start, so that the property is not built twice.

The order matters more than the split does. Grading, drainage and anything that has to run under a patio or a walkway goes first, even when the visible part of that area is years away. Sleeves for irrigation and lighting are inexpensive while the ground is open and costly once there is concrete over them. Planting often makes a good later phase, since plants fill in over time regardless of when they go in.

Two things to know before you plan around it. Each phase is its own agreement with its own price, and that price is set when the phase is priced rather than years in advance. Phasing also costs somewhat more in total than doing the same work at once, because the setup and cleanup happen more than once. It is still the right answer for plenty of projects.

entries.question: Why do I have to pay for a design? Can't you just draw something up?
entries.answer:
Because the design is real work, and it is the part that makes everything after it accurate. Before you pay anything, you get a complimentary concept and a written planning budget: a range to plan around, not a bid. That is enough to decide whether the project is worth going further with. It is not enough to build from.

The paid design step is what turns that concept into something buildable. Your property is measured in detail and drawn to scale. Levels, drainage and access get worked out. Plants and materials get chosen and drawn in place. Those hours are the same hours whether we end up building the project or not, so they are sold as their own step rather than folded into a construction price you have not agreed to yet.

Design is covered by its own signed agreement, separate from any construction contract. You see the scope and the fee in writing before you commit to it.

entries.question: How much do you charge for design?
entries.answer:
Design is priced as a percentage of the construction price, and the band is 10 to 15 percent. That is a common way landscape design is priced, and it is the same band printed on the planning budget you receive before any of this is decided, so you can work out roughly what design will run as soon as you have a construction range.

Where a project lands inside that band depends on how much design there is to do: how many separate areas are in scope, how much grading and drainage has to be resolved, how much irrigation, and whether anything needs outside review. A single planting bed and a whole-property renovation are not the same amount of drawing.

We do not put a design fee in front of you before there is a construction range to apply it to, which is why the complimentary concept and the planning budget come first. The fee, and exactly what it covers, go into the design agreement before you sign it.

entries.question: If I hire you to build it, does the design fee come off the construction price?
entries.answer:
No. The design fee is not credited toward construction, and it is not refunded when you build with us. We say that plainly and early because plenty of clients expect it to be credited, and contract signing is the worst possible moment to find out otherwise.

The reason is straightforward. Design and construction are two separate pieces of work, and each carries its own price. The design hours are spent before a shovel moves, and they are spent whether or not you go ahead. If the fee were credited, the construction price would simply have to carry those hours somewhere you could not see them. We would rather show you both numbers and let you judge each one on its own.

What the fee buys is a plan drawn from real measurements of your property, and a construction price built from that plan instead of from a guess.

entries.question: What do I actually get for the design fee, and do I own the drawings?
entries.answer:
You get a measured plan set for your property: a site plan drawn to scale from real measurements, the layout of paving, walls, steps and beds, a planting plan showing what goes where, irrigation and drainage resolved, and materials specified closely enough to price and build from. You also get the firm construction number that comes out of those plans, which is something a concept sketch cannot produce.

On ownership, the position we recommend and expect to put in writing is this: you receive the drawings and are free to keep them and use them for your property, and GMZ retains the copyright in the drawings themselves. That language is being finalized now.

So ask to see the ownership clause in the design agreement before you sign, and if it is not in there yet, ask for it. A design you paid for should come with a written answer about what you can do with it.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm the ownership and copyright language for design deliverables: whether the client receives the drawings outright, whether GMZ retains copyright, and what use of them is permitted. Nothing is written today, and this must match whatever is decided about taking drawings to another contractor.

entries.question: How long does the design take?
entries.answer:
For a straightforward residential project, weeks rather than months. That is our recommended position and we are in the middle of committing it to writing, so treat it as an honest expectation rather than a published term.

The clock starts when your property is measured, not when you sign. What drives it after that is mostly on the decision side: how many areas are in scope, how quickly plant and material selections get settled, and whether anything needs outside review. A design where the choices land quickly moves quickly, and one that waits on a decision waits.

Ask for a target presentation date to be written into the design agreement. Any date we give you should be one you can hold us to.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm the design timeline GMZ will state publicly: whether it is published as a range, written as a per-project target date in each design agreement, or not published at all. No term exists today.

entries.question: What if I don't like the first design you show me?
entries.answer:
You say so, and we revise it. Nobody gets a yard right on the first try, and the first presentation exists to be reacted to. We would far rather hear that a plan is wrong on paper than watch it get built.

How many rounds of revision are included is being settled now. What we recommend, and what we would write, is two rounds included in the design fee, with anything beyond that priced in writing before we start on it. There is a distinction worth naming: moving a patio, changing a plant palette or reworking a bed line is a revision. Adding a whole new area of the property, or changing what the project is, is new scope, and it moves both the design and the construction number.

Ask what your agreement includes before you sign it, and get the answer in the document rather than in conversation.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm how many revision rounds are included in the design fee, what counts as a revision versus new scope, and how additional rounds are handled and priced. Nothing is written today; the recommended position above is two included rounds.

entries.question: If I pay for the design, can I take the drawings to another contractor?
entries.answer:
Our recommended position is yes, once the design fee is paid in full and with the drawings used for your own property only. That is not settled policy yet, so ask for it to be stated in the design agreement. We would rather earn the construction work on price and workmanship than by holding your plans.

Two things are worth knowing before you do it. A price from another contractor on the same drawings is often not the same thing as ours: the specification, the material grades and how the work is sequenced all move the number, so compare what is actually included rather than just the totals. And whoever builds it carries the workmanship for it. We cannot stand behind construction we did not do.

If another price comes back materially lower, tell us and ask why. There is almost always a nameable reason, and it is much better to find it before the work starts than after.
entries.decisionNote: Sensitive. Confirm whether clients may take GMZ design drawings to another contractor for pricing or construction, and on what conditions: design fee paid in full, use limited to the client's own property, and whether GMZ's name comes off the drawings. Must be consistent with the ownership and copyright language in the design agreement.

entries.question: I already have plans from a landscape architect. Will you build from them?
entries.answer:
Yes. Building to someone else's plans is one of the normal ways a project comes to us, alongside designing it ourselves. There is no design fee in that case, because we are not doing the design.

What we need from you is the full set: the plan, the plant list, and any grading, drainage or construction details that exist. It helps considerably if whoever drew it is reachable for questions. We walk the property and check the drawings against the ground before we price anything. Where a plan does not match the site, and that does happen, you hear about it then, not halfway through construction.

One line worth being clear on: the person who designed it carries the design, and we carry the build. If a detail will not work as drawn, we will say so and propose a fix rather than build something we think is wrong and leave you with it.

entries.question: What's actually included in the price, and what isn't?
entries.answer:
Both are listed in writing in the bid, before you sign anything. Included is every item of work we have priced: the materials and their level, the labor, the equipment, the haul-off and the daily site services. Excluded is named just as plainly, item by item. On a residential landscape job the usual exclusions are permit fees, arborist reports, work inside the house, utility upgrades, rock or buried concrete that could not be seen from the surface, and anything the plan does not show.

A named exclusion is more honest than a padded number. If we quietly added money to cover things that might not happen, you would pay for them whether or not they happened, and you would have no way to tell how much of your price was real work and how much was insurance against a maybe. Naming an exclusion tells you exactly where your price ends and lets you decide what to do about it: bring the item in now, price it separately, or accept the risk knowingly.

Read the exclusions page first. It is the shortest page in the document and it is where nearly every contractor dispute actually lives. If something you assumed was included is sitting on that page, ask us before you sign and we will price it.

entries.question: Why is the bid different from the budget range you gave me earlier?
entries.answer:
Because the earlier number was a planning range built from a walk-through and a concept, and this one is built from a measured site and materials you have chosen. That is the entire difference, and it is the reason this number can be committed to and the first one could not.

Three things move it, and we name which ones moved yours. The site gets measured, so quantities stop being read off photographs. Materials get chosen, and on hardscape the gap between a basic paver and natural stone over the same area is a multiple, not a percentage. And the scope settles: demolition and haul-off come in or stay out, and drainage gets assessed rather than assumed. Any of those three can move a number in either direction, and the measured price sometimes comes in under the planning range.

If the bid lands outside the range you were given, we tell you before you open the document and we name the reason. Every real gap has one. A number that moved for no reason anybody can name means we got something wrong, and we would rather find that ourselves than have you find it.

entries.question: How long is this price good for?
entries.answer:
Until the date printed on the face of the bid. We normally set that at thirty days from the day we issue it, and after that we re-check material prices before we honor the number.

Thirty days is not an arbitrary deadline. Material prices in this trade move on their own schedule: stone, lumber, concrete and plant stock especially. The prices sitting behind your number carry expiry dates of their own. A month is long enough for you to think it over and short enough that we are not committing to a price nobody can still buy.

If you go past the date, tell us rather than assuming the number is dead. Most of the time it barely moves and we simply re-issue it. Where something has genuinely changed, we show you which line changed and why, instead of handing you a new total and letting you guess.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm the price-validity window before this publishes: whether thirty days from issue is the standing rule, what the printed expiry date is measured from, and what GMZ does when a client comes back after it lapses. Nothing on this is currently written down, and the draft stated thirty days as settled policy.

entries.question: Can you price a couple of different material options so I can compare?
entries.answer:
Yes, and on the big items we would rather you asked. Tell us which two levels you want to see and we price the identical scope both ways, so the only thing that changes between the two documents is the material.

We do this because the material level is the largest single lever in a landscape price, and there is no honest midpoint to guess at. Pricing one tier and calling it the answer hides the decision from you. Seeing the same patio priced two ways puts the trade in front of you in dollars, which is where it belongs. We will also tell you where we think the money works hardest: a smaller area in the better material usually reads better than a large area in the cheaper one, and there are places where nobody will ever notice the difference.

The same applies to phasing. If the whole scope is more than you want to commit to now, we can price it in stages, so the parts that only happen once go in together: base, drainage and irrigation lines. The visible surfaces follow later. Tell us at bid time, because phasing decided after the crew has left costs more than phasing designed in.

entries.question: Who pulls the permits, and who pays for them?
entries.answer:
GMZ files the permit and manages the inspections as the licensed contractor of record, and the fee itself is billed to you as a separate line at whatever the town charges, not folded into the price.

Most residential landscape work on the Peninsula needs no permit at all. The work that commonly does: a retaining wall over a certain height, structures you can stand under, electrical, gas lines, anything that changes how water leaves your property, and on larger planting and irrigation projects, the state's landscape water-efficiency review. Every town on the Peninsula sets its own thresholds and its own timeline, so we tell you at bid time which of these we expect to apply to your job and roughly what it does to the start date.

The fee is excluded from the price rather than estimated into it for a simple reason: the town sets it, it varies by jurisdiction and by valuation, and we cannot know it before the application goes in. Naming a guess and then correcting it later is worse than naming it as a pass-through from the start.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm: (a) that GMZ files permits and manages inspections as standard rather than case by case, and (b) that permit fees are passed through to the client as a separate line at the town's cost rather than carried in the price. Neither is currently written down.

entries.question: How far out are you booked?
entries.answer:
It changes month to month, so ask us and we will give you the real date rather than a comfortable one. We check the work already committed against the calendar before we promise a start, which is why we do not post a booking window on the website: a number published there is wrong by the time most people read it.

What does not change is how the queue works. A start date is held by a signed contract, not by a conversation, and until the paperwork is done your slot is not yours. We will say that plainly rather than let you assume otherwise and then find out in week six. Materials with a long lead are ordered as soon as the contract is in: specimen trees, stone from a particular quarry, custom metal. That ordering window, rather than crew availability, is often what sets the earliest honest start.

If you have a hard date, an event, a house sale, a school year, a permit clock, tell us in the first conversation. It changes what we recommend, it sometimes changes the sequence of the build, and occasionally it is the reason we tell you we are not the right contractor for this one.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm what GMZ publishes about lead time: whether a current booking window goes on the site at all, who updates it and how often, and whether the stated rule is that a start date is held only by a signed contract and deposit.

entries.question: How long is my yard going to be a construction site?
entries.short: How long the yard's torn up
entries.answer:
Longer than the number of working days on the schedule, and you should hear that from us now rather than discover it in week three. A build is not continuous work. There are days of machines and noise, then a quiet stretch waiting on a concrete cure, an inspection or a delivery, then noise again. Your yard is out of use from the first day of demolition to the last day of cleanup, quiet stretches included.

The shape of it is fairly consistent. The roughest part is at the front: demolition, grading and drainage, which is where the noise, the dust and the machine traffic all live. Expect part of your driveway or street frontage to be staging for material and debris, and we will tell you which part before we start. If plants are staying, irrigation may be off for a stretch and we will tell you what needs hand watering and when. The back half of a job is quieter and finer: planting, irrigation adjustment, lighting and cleanup.

You get a working schedule at the pre-construction meeting and an update once a week on the same day: what changed, what is next, and anything that needs a decision from you. Three things move a landscape schedule: weather, inspections, and what we find underground. Each has its own answer in this list, and none of them is a surprise we spring on you at the end.

entries.question: How much do you need up front, and when do I pay the rest?
entries.answer:
Less than most people expect, because California limits it. On a home improvement contract the down payment cannot exceed the lesser of $1,000 or 10 percent of the contract price. That is state law and it exists to protect you. Any residential contractor asking for a third up front is not following it, and that is worth knowing whoever you hire.

For the rest, payments fall due against milestones as work is completed, never on a calendar. A payment is triggered by something finished that you can walk out and look at, and each milestone is named in the contract before you sign, so there is no interpretation left for later. The final payment comes after the walkthrough and after the punch list is cleared, not before.

One thing that catches people out: the design step runs under its own separate signed agreement, with its own terms, and it is paid separately from construction. The design fee is not a deposit on the build and it is not credited toward it. That is the single most common assumption clients bring to this conversation, so we answer it early rather than at signing.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm the milestone payment schedule for design/build contracts: how many payments, what completed event triggers each one, what share of the contract sits in the final payment, and whether final payment is formally tied to a cleared punch list. Nothing is currently standardized and jobs vary. Also confirm what the final walkthrough consists of, since this answer ties the last payment to it. The $1,000 / 10 percent figure is the California statutory limit on home improvement down payments, not a GMZ number.

entries.question: What's a change order, and how do I avoid getting hit with a pile of them?
entries.answer:
A change order is a written amendment to the contract, priced and signed by both of us before the work happens, covering anything that was not in the original scope. Nothing is added to your bill without one. If anyone on a job site tells you a change is no problem and it never appears in writing, that is not generosity; it is a bill you have not seen yet.

There are three causes and two of them are avoidable. Scope you add mid-job, which is fine and is what change orders are for: you see the wall going up and want it longer. Decisions made late, a surface chosen after the base is already in. And genuine unknowns underground, which is the third and is the reason the exclusions page exists at all.

How to keep the count near zero: choose your materials before we start rather than during, read the exclusions page and ask about anything you assumed was included, let us assess the drainage instead of assuming the existing setup is fine, and make your list of while-you're-here additions before the contract rather than in week two. Adding something at bid time is nearly always cheaper than adding it after the crew has moved past that part of the yard and has to come back to it.

entries.question: Who is actually going to be on my property, and do I need to be home?
entries.answer:
GMZ's own crew does the work under our supervision, and no, you do not need to be home once we have what we need to get in and get water. Where a trade requires its own license, electrical work being the usual one, that portion is done by a licensed subcontractor working under our contract, and we tell you in advance which parts those are and when they are coming.

What we need from you comes up at the pre-construction meeting, before the first truck arrives: gate code or key, where the water and power are, where we can park and stage material, hours that work for you and your neighbors, anything we should know about pets and children, and one person on your side who can answer a question by phone during the day. That last one matters more than being present. A decision that sits over a weekend can hold the schedule up for a day.

There are three moments worth being there for. Layout on the first day, when the shapes get marked on the ground and are cheap to move. The irrigation and controller handover, which takes a few minutes in person and a long email otherwise. And the walkthrough at the end. Everything in between runs perfectly well on a weekly update and photographs.

entries.question: What happens when it rains?
entries.answer:
Work that rain would ruin stops; work it would not carries on. Compaction, concrete, paving, grading and planting into saturated soil all fail if you force them, so those move. Fence posts, irrigation repair, pruning, cleanup and most maintenance visits go ahead in the wet.

A weather delay is not a change order and does not add anything to your price. It moves the schedule, and we tell you the same week what moved and what the new sequence looks like. What we will not do is push a weather-sensitive task through because a date was promised. A patio set on soft base looks fine for one season and then tells on you for years afterward, and that is our problem as much as yours.

From late autumn through early spring we build float into the schedule for this rather than pretending the season is dry, and we leave the site safe ahead of a storm: exposed soil covered, open trenches protected, and water still leaving your property the way it is supposed to.

entries.question: What happens if you dig and find something you weren't expecting?
entries.answer:
We stop, photograph it, show it to you, price the fix and get your signature before we carry on. You will not learn about it from the final invoice.

What actually turns up in Peninsula yards: an old slab or footing under the lawn, rock, an abandoned irrigation line, a septic remnant, tree roots at a size where an arborist ought to look at them, a drain that goes nowhere, and utility lines that are not where any map says. None of it is visible from the surface, which is precisely why it sits on the exclusions page instead of inside your price. If we padded every bid for things that are usually not there, every client would be paying for the unlucky ones.

We cut the odds where we can. We call the utility locate in before any digging, we assess the drainage rather than assume it, and where we have real doubt about what is under a surface we say so at bid time and suggest digging a test hole before you sign. A test hole costs a fraction of what the same discovery costs in week two with a crew standing on it.

entries.question: Do you call 811 before digging, or is that something I have to arrange?
entries.answer:
Yes, every job, and no, you do not arrange it. GMZ places the utility locate request before any digging on your property. It is free, it is required in California, and the marks have to be on the ground before a shovel goes in. The request carries a required notice period, so it goes in ahead of the first day of work rather than being called in that morning.

One limit is worth knowing. The locate service marks public utilities in the work area by color: gas, electric, water, communications. It does not mark private lines, and Peninsula properties are full of them: the run out to a detached garage or shed, pool equipment, landscape lighting, a well, a septic line. Those sit on your side of the meter and no agency holds a record of them. Tell us anything you know about or suspect, even vaguely, and we hand-dig wherever a private line is likely.

Skipping the call is how a routine Tuesday becomes an incident: a struck gas line, an evacuated block, a neighborhood without power, and a homeowner in the middle of a conversation they did not sign up for. There is no version of this job we do faster by not doing it.

entries.question: What's your warranty if something you built fails?
entries.answer:
One year on workmanship from the date your project is complete is the term we work to, and we will put it in writing in your contract before you sign. It covers the work of our hands: paving that settles, a wall that moves, a drain that will not drain, a leaking irrigation fitting, a light that fails because of how it was wired. If it is our installation, we come back and put it right at no cost to you.

It does not cover plants, which we answer separately, and it does not cover things outside our control: another trade working the same ground after we leave, a change somebody else made, storm damage, or a root from a neighboring tree. Where materials and equipment carry a manufacturer's coverage, that coverage is yours and we will help you use it.

One thing to be straight about: the written warranty page is still being finalized, so do not rely on a verbal term from anybody, including us. Ask for the current warranty language, read it, and get it attached to your contract before work starts.
entries.decisionNote: Nothing is written today. This is the canonical warranty decision and 'Who to call if something fails' and 'Plants and the maintenance account' both depend on it. Confirm the workmanship warranty term (recommended: one year from substantial completion), the exclusion list, whether it transfers if the home is sold, and approve the written warranty document before this answer is published.

entries.question: A few of the new plants died. Will you replace them?
entries.answer:
Not automatically, and we would rather say that up front than surprise you later. GMZ does not guarantee plants after installation. The reason is watering: once the garden is yours, we do not control how much water it gets or when it gets it, and a plant's first year is decided almost entirely by that.

What we do stand behind is our part of it: sound nursery stock, correct planting depth, prepared soil, and irrigation that was working when we handed it over. If a plant fails because of how it was planted, or because a zone was never actually running, that one is ours and we replace it. Call us and we will come and look.

The exception is when GMZ holds your maintenance account. Then the watering and the aftercare are ours, we are in the garden every week or every other week, and a plant that fails under our care is ours to make right. That is the honest reason the two things are connected, not a sales pitch.

entries.question: Something stopped working after you finished. Who do I call?
entries.short: Who to call if something fails
entries.answer:
Call the office number on your paperwork and ask for the person who ran your job. That is the fastest route, because they know the ground, the zones and what is buried where. Please do not route it through a crew member's personal phone: work that is not written down at the office is work that gets lost.

Have three things ready when you call: what is failing, when it started, and a photo. For irrigation, the zone number if you know it. That is usually enough to tell whether it is a fitting, a valve, the controller or a plant that was never getting water, and it decides whether we bring a truck or talk you through it on the phone.

Then we come and look. If it is our workmanship, we put it right at no cost to you. If it turns out to be something else, a repair somebody else made, storm damage, or a plant that dried out, we will tell you plainly and give you a price to put it right rather than quietly adding it to a bill. Water against the house or a leak you cannot shut off should be called in the same day.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm whether GMZ publishes a response commitment for post-completion callbacks (for example: contact within two business days, urgent water issues same day), whether one named point of contact is assigned per job, and whether the diagnostic visit is free regardless of who turns out to be at fault. Also confirm the workmanship warranty term before publishing, since this answer promises free repair of GMZ workmanship.

entries.question: What actually happens on the last day? Is there a final walkthrough?
entries.answer:
Yes, and our position is that it should be the same on every job: a walkthrough with you, on site, ending in a written punch list. We walk the whole project together, you point out anything that is not right, we write each item down with a date next to it, and you keep a copy. Nothing on that list is a favor. It is part of the job you already bought, and the list is not closed until you say it is.

One honest caveat: this has varied job to job, and we are standardizing it. If it matters to you, ask for it before you sign and we will put it in the contract in plain words.

The last day is also when we offer maintenance. That is a separate conversation with its own agreement, its own schedule and its own terms, not something folded into your construction contract, and you are free to say no.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm that a walkthrough with a written punch list is standard on every design/build job: who attends, who signs it, whether both parties keep a copy, and how long GMZ has to clear punch items before the job is called complete.

entries.question: What does a brand new garden actually need in its first year?
entries.answer:
Water, delivered the right way, matters more than everything else combined in the first year. New plants are growing roots, not showing off. Water deeply and less often so the moisture goes down and the roots follow it; short daily sprinkles keep roots at the surface and make a plant that cannot survive its first hot week. If something looks stressed between cycles, hand water that plant rather than raising the schedule for the whole garden.

Two other things carry most of the rest. Keep mulch topped up and pulled back off the stems, and pull weeds while they are small, because freshly worked soil grows them fast. Do not push fertilizer in the first season and do not prune new shrubs hard: both work against a plant that is trying to root. Expect some settling in new beds and paths, and expect a few plants to sit and sulk for a season before they move.

By the second summer the garden can run on a normal schedule. The first year is the one that decides whether it gets there, which is also why we always offer to maintain it ourselves.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm whether a written closeout package (plan copy, plant list, watering schedule, care guide) is handed over on every design/build job, and whether the thirty-day and six-month follow-up calls become standard practice. This answer currently promises care guidance that no document delivers yet. The same closeout package is promised in 'Running your irrigation controller', 'Using someone else' and 'Plants and the maintenance account'.

entries.question: How do I run the new irrigation controller? I don't want to kill everything.
entries.answer:
Mostly you do not have to run it: we program it before we hand it over and we walk you through it on site, so you are not working it out alone. The short version is: leave the schedule we set. It is built for your zones, your soil and the season you took the garden over in.

A few things worth knowing. Zones water early in the morning, before the heat and the wind. Drip zones in the beds run long and only a couple of times a week, because they put water down slowly. Lawn and spray zones run shorter and more often. If you have a smart Wi-Fi controller, it adjusts itself with the weather, so a stretch of rain or heat does not need you to touch anything. Use the manual or single zone function when you want to run one zone and see where the water is actually going.

Change the schedule twice a year rather than constantly: down in the fall, up in late spring. If you are not sure, call before you change it. A controller that somebody reset is a common reason a new garden dies, and it is the easiest one to avoid.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm whether every job leaves with a written irrigation zone map and a copy of the programmed seasonal schedule, and whether later reprogramming or a seasonal adjustment visit is included, billed by the hour, or available only under a maintenance account.

entries.question: What do you actually do on a maintenance visit?
entries.answer:
A visit is routine care: the work that keeps a garden looking the way it did the week we finished it. On a typical residential property that means mowing and edging where there is lawn, cleaning down the hard surfaces, weeding the beds, light seasonal pruning and shaping of shrubs, perennials and grasses, and hauling away the green waste we generate that day.

We also walk the irrigation while we are there. A head knocked out of line, a drip line pulled loose by a dog, a zone that quietly stopped running: those are easy to catch on a regular visit and painful to find after a month of dry weather has taken the plants on that zone. We adjust controller run times as the seasons change, and we tell you what we saw.

We work from a standing list for your property rather than from whatever catches the eye that morning. If we see something that falls outside the visit, we tell you about it instead of doing it and billing you afterward.

entries.question: How do you price maintenance?
entries.answer:
On how much your property takes to service properly, and how often we come. We walk the property before pricing anything: how much lawn there is, how much planted bed, how much pruning it will want across a year, how much green waste comes off it, and how easily equipment moves around it.

That produces one set price per visit, agreed before the first visit, which does not move from week to week because one visit ran longer than another. Two things sit outside it: work that is not part of routine care, and materials we bring for you. Both are priced and approved before we do them, never added to a bill after the fact.

We do not price maintenance off a photo or a look from the street. A number produced that way is a number for a property nobody has seen, and it changes once someone finally walks it.

entries.question: Should I be on a weekly or an every-other-week schedule?
entries.answer:
Weekly if you have lawn, a lot of planted bed, or you want the property to look tidy every day of the week. Every other week works well for gardens that are mostly established shrubs, groundcover, gravel or decomposed granite, where growth is slow and there is not much to pick up.

The honest test is the growing season, not the winter. From spring into early summer, a lawn on a two-week cycle can look shaggy well before the next visit, and the beds put on enough growth that the visit stops being maintenance and starts being catch-up. Plenty of properties want weekly through the growing months and settle into every other week once things slow down.

If you are unsure, tell us which way you are leaning and we will give you an honest read after a few visits. Changing cadence changes your service agreement and your price, so we confirm it with you in writing rather than simply showing up more often.

entries.question: What day will you come, and is it the same day every time?
entries.answer:
Yes, you get a fixed day of the week and we keep it. Routes are built by area so the crew is working rather than driving, which means your day is not very moveable once it is set. If you need a particular day, say so before we start and we will tell you what the route allows.

We give you a day, not an arrival time. The stops ahead of you vary, so the hour moves. You do not need to be home. What we do need is reliable access on your day: a gate code or a key if there is a lock, dogs secured, and a working outdoor spigot.

Weather and holidays are the two exceptions. Most maintenance work goes ahead in light rain. When conditions make the work pointless or damaging, we move the visit within the same week where the route allows it, and we tell you rather than leaving you to notice.

entries.question: What is not included in maintenance?
entries.answer:
Anything that changes the garden rather than keeping it as it is. Routine care is in: mowing, edging, blowing down hard surfaces, weeding, seasonal pruning of shrubs and perennials, hauling the green waste from that visit, and checking the irrigation as we go. What follows is out, and it is a long list on purpose.

Not included: tree work beyond what can be reached safely from the ground, and anything needing a climb, a lift or a chipper; structural or heavy renovation pruning; removing plants, replacing plants, and any new planting; seasonal color changeouts; lawn renovation, reseeding, sod, aeration and dethatching; irrigation repair beyond a quick fix at a head or an emitter, which means valves, wiring, mainline breaks, new zones and controller replacement are all separate; fertilizer, compost and soil amendment programs; pest, disease and weed treatments calling for a licensed applicator; storm cleanup and debris we did not generate; heavy leaf drop through the fall; mulch and gravel top-ups, which are a material purchase; pressure washing, gutters and roofs; hardscape, fence, deck, lighting and drainage repair; pet waste; moving furniture and planters; and holiday lighting.

None of that is a refusal. Much of it we can take on as separate work, and where a job calls for a licensed specialty trade we bring in the right one. Either way it is priced and approved separately, so nobody meets it on an invoice. Writing the line down where you can see it is easier for both of us than arguing about it later. The other half is what we need from you: access on your day, pets contained, water available, and any HOA rules that limit what can be cut or removed.

entries.question: Will the same people come every week?
entries.answer:
Usually, yes. A route is worked by the same team week after week, and that is deliberate. They learn where the valve box is, which shrub the dog gets behind, which corner holds water, and how you like the beds edged. A property served by whoever happened to be free that morning gets maintained to the average of everyone who has ever been there.

We will not promise the identical people on every single visit, because people take vacation, get sick and sometimes move on, and that is a promise we would end up breaking. When somebody covers, they work from the record for your property: the photos and notes from the first assessment visit, and what has been done since. A covering team should not arrive blind.

If a visit is ever done poorly, tell us that week rather than months later. It is easy to put right while everyone still remembers the day.

entries.question: Am I locked into a contract, and how do I cancel?
entries.answer:
You are not locked into a long commitment, and our position is that you should be able to end it in writing with no penalty. There is a written service agreement, and it is a separate document from any construction contract you may have with us. It states the scope of a visit, the cadence, your day, the price, what is included, what is not, and how either side ends it. Maintenance is a standing obligation rather than a job with a finish line, so it needs terms a construction contract does not have.

We hold ourselves to the same notice in the other direction. An agreement should keep a schedule honest, not trap anybody. The exact notice period and the renewal terms are being finalized and will be printed on the face of the agreement, so you read them before you sign rather than after.

If something is not working, the better first move is usually a conversation. A cancellation is often a scope problem or a cadence problem that nobody raised while it was still easy to fix.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm the maintenance agreement terms before this answer publishes: the notice period for cancellation by either side, the agreement term and renewal terms, and whether an annual price review is stated on the face of the agreement. Nothing is written yet, so this answer states the recommended position rather than a settled one.

entries.question: Are you taking on new maintenance clients right now?
entries.answer:
Ask us, because the answer depends on where you are. Maintenance runs as routes: a group of properties in the same area on the same day. A property that sits well off an existing route is hard to serve well, and we would rather decline it than take it and become the crew that arrives late and leaves early.

So the useful thing to tell us first is your town and which part of it you are in, before anything about the yard. If you are near a route we already run, this is a short conversation. If you are not, we will say so plainly instead of putting you on a list that goes nowhere.

We are based in Redwood City and work the San Francisco Peninsula.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm whether GMZ is open to new maintenance accounts right now, and which towns or route days are open, so this answer can say yes or no instead of 'ask us'.

entries.question: Can you just come once and clean the place up?
entries.answer:
Sometimes, and it depends on the schedule. Tell us what you are actually after, because a one-time cleanup is a different thing from maintenance: a defined job with a start and a finish, priced on the work in front of us rather than a recurring visit on a route.

Our position is that these are worth doing when they fit the week, and especially where a property is heading toward ongoing service or a build. A standalone cleanup dropped into a full week displaces work already promised to somebody else, so the answer is sometimes no, and that is better said early than late.

Whether we offer cleanups as a standing service is being settled. Send a few photos along with your town and we will tell you straight.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm whether GMZ offers one-time or seasonal cleanups as a standalone service, and on what conditions (route fit, existing clients only, or certain seasons only).

entries.question: You built my garden. Do you maintain it too?
entries.answer:
Yes, and we offer it at handover on every project we build. The first year is when a new garden is most easily lost: irrigation needs adjusting as roots go down, the first prunings set the shape for years, and the watering schedule that was right in May is wrong by September. None of that is difficult, but it has to actually happen.

It is a separate engagement rather than a continuation of the build. Your construction contract ends when the work is accepted. Maintenance begins after that under its own service agreement, with its own schedule and its own terms, because a recurring service and a fixed-price construction job carry different obligations on both sides.

We put the maintenance price in front of you at handover so you can decide with the number in hand instead of being asked in the abstract. No is a normal answer and it changes nothing about the build.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm what happens at handover, since it currently varies by job: whether the maintenance price is presented at the final walkthrough, who presents it, and what else that walkthrough covers. Until that is settled this answer says 'at handover' and does not name a final walkthrough step.

entries.question: Do I have to use you for maintenance after you build it?
entries.answer:
No. Hire whoever you like, keep the gardener you already have, or look after it yourself. We will not make it awkward.

What we hand over is built to work for whoever ends up caring for the garden: a copy of the plan, the plant list, the irrigation zone map with the controller settings we programmed, and a care guide covering what needs doing and roughly when. Give that to your gardener on the first day and they start well ahead of where most people start.

One thing we would rather state than bury: our position on plants is different depending on who is doing the watering. That has its own answer, and the reason is about control rather than pressure.
entries.decisionNote: This answer promises the same written closeout package as 'Caring for a new garden' and 'Plants and the maintenance account': plan copy, plant list, irrigation zone map with programmed settings, and a care guide. No document delivers that yet. Confirm the closeout package before this publishes, or the promise has to come out of all three answers together.

entries.question: Why aren't the plants guaranteed unless you're the ones maintaining the garden?
entries.answer:
Because once we hand over, we no longer control the watering, and watering is what decides whether plants live. We can choose the right plant for the exposure, prepare the soil, plant it correctly and set the controller before we leave. What happens next is outside our hands: a controller switched off for a trip, a zone that stops running and nobody notices, a mower through a drip line, a hot stretch in the first September. So we do not guarantee plants after installation, and we say that before you sign rather than after something dies.

When we hold the maintenance account, that reason goes away. We are the ones on the property, we are the ones adjusting run times through the season, and we are the ones who see a plant under stress while it can still be saved. Standing behind planting is reasonable where we control the conditions and unreasonable where we do not. What exactly that covers is being written down now, and it will sit in the agreement rather than in a conversation.

If it still reads as a sales pitch, measure it against what a client who goes elsewhere gets: the plan, the plant list, the irrigation zone map, the controller settings and the care guide, with nothing held back. We would rather the garden survive under somebody else's care than sell an account nobody wanted.
entries.decisionNote: Confirm the written warranty before this publishes: the workmanship term (recommended one year from completion), that plants are excluded with the reason stated, and what, if anything, GMZ commits to on planting where GMZ holds the maintenance account. Nothing is written yet, so no term or coverage is stated here as fact.

entries.question: I'm already a maintenance client. Can you build something for me?
entries.answer:
Yes, and it runs the same way it would for anyone else: a site consultation, a complimentary concept, a preliminary budget with a planning range, then a separate signed design agreement if you want measured drawings and a firm price. Being a maintenance client does not shortcut the design step and does not change how the work is priced.

What it does change is how much we already know. We have been on your property every week or two, so we know the irrigation, the soil, where water sits after a wet winter and what has failed there before. That usually makes the concept sharper and the list of open questions shorter, and it takes some of the guesswork out of the budget range.

Your maintenance continues during the build. Where construction touches ground the crew normally services, we will tell you what happens to those visits for that stretch rather than leaving you to work it out from an invoice. The two agreements stay separate: the build is a construction contract, the maintenance is a service agreement, and neither absorbs the other.
